title: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage to Mecca, 1324–25
summary: The king of Mali crossed the Sahara with a great company and a fortune in gold, camped by the pyramids in July 1324, spent three months in Cairo, and went on with the Egyptian pilgrim caravan to Medina and Mecca. Home by Cairo, where he borrowed to pay his way, and by Gao and Timbuktu, which the later chronicles say came under Mali as he passed. Only Giza, Cairo, Mecca, Gao and Timbuktu are recorded for him; the stops in the desert are the usual drawing, or a reckoning of the caravan roads. Some accounts have him home in 1326.

legs.source: the usual drawing of the hajj road; no source read names a stop before Cairo
legs.note: the capital is placed at Niani by convention; its site is debated, and recent historians put it elsewhere on the upper Niger or doubt Niani was inhabited then (Wikipedia, Mali Empire). The departure date is not recorded.

legs.source: the usual drawing, by the Taghaza salt mines, which Mali held under Musa (Wikipedia, Mali Empire)
legs.note: whether the caravan went by Taghaza or straight to Tuat is not recorded

legs.source: Giza is recorded; Tuat and the road between are the usual drawing and a reckoning
legs.note: Ghadames, Awjila and Siwa only give the line its shape: they are the oases on the caravan road to Egypt, and no source read names them for Musa. Tripoli and the coast road by Barqa would serve as well.

legs.source: Wikipedia, Mansa Musa: three days by the pyramids, then across the Nile on 19 July
Wikipedia, Mansa Musa: he left Cairo on 18 October with the official caravan, and gave gifts at Medina and Mecca
legs.note: the road by Suez, Nakhl and Aqaba is the Egyptian pilgrims' usual one, not recorded for Musa; whether he came to Medina before Mecca or after is not recorded

legs.source: Wikipedia, Mansa Musa: he stayed on after the pilgrimage and came home apart from the main caravan, losing many of his people to cold, hunger and raiders before Suez
Cairo is recorded, and Gao by the Tarikh al-Sudan; the road between is a reckoning
legs.note: Awjila, Murzuq in the Fezzan, Ghat and Takedda only give the line its shape: they are the stages of the caravan road from Egypt to the Niger, and no source read names them for Musa. He may as well have come back by Tuat and Walata.

legs.source: the Tarikh al-Sudan has both towns submit to Musa on his way home (Wikipedia, Mansa Musa); the way between follows the Niger
nobody records the last stretch home; the line follows the Niger up to the capital
legs.note: Djenne only gives the line its shape; the capital is placed at Niani by convention

events.label: Camp at Giza, and into Cairo
events.text: He camped three days by the pyramids and crossed the Nile into Cairo on 19 July 1324, to stay three months. The sources count his company at thousands, then ten thousand (Ibn al-Wardi, the late 1340s), then 60,000 with 500 slaves bearing gold wands (the Tarikh al-Sudan, 1655), with 80 camels or more carrying gold. The 12,000 enslaved attendants dressed in silk come from al-Qalqashandi in 1412, as something 'it is said'; Isaac Samuel reads the figure as rhetoric, not a muster, and finds the earliest accounts speak of free companions, the only slaves named being Turks the sultan gave him.

events.label: The gold, and the price of gold
events.text: He left no emir or officer of the court without a load of gold, and the people of Cairo made great profits buying and selling with his caravan. Al-Umari, in Cairo some years later, wrote that they traded away so much gold that its price fell and had not recovered twelve years on: the mithqal, worth 25 dirhams, went for under 22.
events.doubt: Warren Schultz finds the fall within the normal swings of gold's value in Mamluk Egypt (Wikipedia)

events.label: Refusing to bow to the sultan
events.source: al-Umari, Masalik al-absar, from the emir Ibn Amir Hajib; the bow from Wikipedia, after Gomez
events.text: The emir sent to meet him urged him to go up to the Citadel to meet the sultan, al-Nasir Muhammad, and he refused again and again: 'I came for the Pilgrimage and nothing else.' Wikipedia, after Gomez, adds that the sultan expected him to prostrate himself, that he refused, and that when at last he bowed he said it was to God alone; the two parted with gifts.

events.label: Mecca
events.text: The pilgrimage of the year 724, which fell about late November 1324. He gave gifts to the people of Mecca and Medina, and stayed on after the rites. In the Great Mosque his pilgrims came to drawn swords with Turkish ones, and he talked his men down.

events.label: Borrowing in Cairo
events.source: Ibn Khaldun, via Wikipedia, Mansa Musa
events.text: Back in Cairo with his gold spent, he borrowed from the city's merchants at high interest. Ibn Khaldun records 50,000 dinars from the Banu l-Kuwayk, and al-Umari and Ibn Khaldun say the lenders were never paid back, or only in part.

events.label: Gao comes under Mali
events.source: Tarikh al-Sudan, via Wikipedia, Mansa Musa
events.text: The Tarikh al-Sudan, written at Timbuktu in the 1650s, says Gao and Timbuktu submitted to Musa as he passed on his way home.
events.doubt: Ibn Khaldun gives the taking of Gao to Musa's general Saghmanja, and Fauvelle doubts that a company of pilgrims could have taken such cities (Wikipedia)

events.label: Timbuktu, al-Sahili and the Djinguereber
events.text: He brought home from the pilgrimage the Andalusi poet Abu Ishaq al-Sahili, who settled in Timbuktu and died there in 1346; Ibn Battuta saw his grave. The Djinguereber mosque was begun at Timbuktu under Musa, about 1327, and the city grew into a centre of learning.
events.doubt: Al-Sahili is long credited with designing the Djinguereber, but Hunwick finds the only work firmly his in the Arabic sources an audience chamber at the capital, paid for with 12,000 mithqals of gold (Wikipedia)
